results.name: lure37_yes_rate_power2_sets
results.description: Yes-rate for target 37 on sets whose examples are all powers of 2 (37 is only in the 'powers of 2, or 37' rule); observed < null means the model over-produces yes to the 37 lure by giving that ad-hoc rule as much prior mass as plain powers of 2.

results.name: rule_inconsistent_yes_rate_rule_sets
results.description: For sets of >=2 examples that some arithmetic rule fully contains, yes-rate for targets that belong to none of those containing rules; observed > null means people keep a residual tendency to say yes outside every consistent rule that the model (near-zero) misses; observed < null means the model's interval mass leaks too much.

results.name: two_example_shared_digit_offdigit_inrange
results.description: For sets of exactly 2 examples sharing a final digit, yes-rate for targets within [min,max] that do not end in that digit; observed < null means the model's size-principle strength (fit mostly on larger sets) is too weak for 2-example sets, so it over-produces interval generalization there.

results.name: power2_target_yes_rate_power2_sets
results.description: Yes-rate for power-of-2 targets not among the examples, on sets whose examples are all powers of 2; observed < null means the model over-generalizes the powers-of-2 rule (people are far more conservative, e.g. 8,64 -> 2,4,16,32 almost always no).

results.name: even_nonmult4_yes_rate_mult4_sets
results.description: For sets of >=2 examples all multiples of 4, yes-rate for even targets that are not multiples of 4; observed > null means the model's size principle is too sharp (people still partly accept the broader 'even' rule), observed < null means too flat.

results.name: interval_only_set_inrange_yes_rate
results.description: For sets of >=2 examples that no arithmetic rule fully contains (only intervals fit), yes-rate for targets within [min,max] of the examples; observed < null means the model over-produces interval generalization for unstructured sets.

results.name: smallest_rule_consistent_yes_rate
results.description: Among sets of >=3 examples that some arithmetic rule fully contains, yes-rate for non-example targets inside the smallest such rule; observed < null means the model is over-confident in rule-consistent generalization (people say yes only ~50-70%, e.g. multiples of 3).
results.code:
# name: smallest_rule_consistent_yes_rate
# description: Among sets of >=3 examples that some arithmetic rule fully contains, yes-rate for non-example targets inside the smallest such rule; observed < null means the model is over-confident in rule-consistent generalization (people say yes only ~50-70%, e.g. multiples of 3).
def _rules():
    N = range(1, 101)
    def isprime(n):
        return n > 1 and all(n % a for a in range(2, int(n ** 0.5) + 1))
    r = {"odd": [n for n in N if n % 2], "even": list(range(2, 101, 2)),
         "primes": [n for n in N if isprime(n)], "squares": [n * n for n in range(1, 11)],
         "cubes": [n ** 3 for n in range(1, 5)], "pow2_not32": [2, 4, 8, 16, 64],
         "pow2_or37": [2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 37, 64]}
    for m in [3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 11, 12]:
        r["mult%d" % m] = list(range(m, 101, m))
    for m in range(2, 11):
        r["pow%d" % m] = [m ** k for k in range(1, 8) if m ** k <= 100]
    for dd in range(10):
        r["ends%d" % dd] = [n for n in N if n % 10 == dd]
        r["contains%d" % dd] = [n for n in N if str(dd) in str(n)]
    names = list(r)
    mem = np.zeros((len(names), 101), dtype=bool)
    for i, k in enumerate(names):
        mem[i, r[k]] = True
    return names, mem


def _prep(df):
    names, mem = _rules()
    codes, uniq = pd.factorize(df["number_set"].astype(str))
    sets = [np.array([int(x) for x in s.split(",")]) for s in uniq]
    setmask = np.array([mem[:, s].all(axis=1) for s in sets])  # (nsets, nrules) rules containing all examples
    t = df["target"].astype(int).to_numpy()
    y = df["rating"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    return names, mem, codes, sets, setmask, t, y


def _rate(y, m):
    return float(y[m].mean()) if m.sum() > 0 else 0.0


def test_statistic(df):
    names, mem, codes, sets, setmask, t, y = _prep(df)
    sizes = mem.sum(axis=1).astype(float)
    big = np.where(setmask, sizes[None, :], np.inf)
    best = big.argmin(axis=1)
    s_ok = np.array([len(s) >= 3 for s in sets]) & setmask.any(axis=1)
    in_rule = mem[best[codes], t]
    notin = np.zeros(len(t), dtype=bool)
    for i, s in enumerate(sets):
        m = codes == i
        notin[m] = ~np.isin(t[m], s)
    return _rate(y, s_ok[codes] & in_rule & notin)

results.name: single_example_yes_rate
results.description: Yes-rate on trials whose set has exactly one example; observed < null means the model over-generalizes from a single example (too much prior mass on broad concepts), observed > null the reverse.
